about:
Painted in Düsseldorf by a German-American who hoped it would stiffen the spines of Europe’s reformers after the failed revolutions of 1848. The scene is the night of December 25, 1776, when Washington crossed the icy Delaware to surprise the Hessian garrison at Trenton.

It is more than twenty-one feet wide. Almost every detail has been picked apart by historians, and none of that has dented it.

Painted in June 1889 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, a few weeks after The Starry Night. Van Gogh thought the cypresses deserved the attention he had given sunflowers, and he counted this among his best summer landscapes.

Nothing in it holds still: the wheat, the olive trees and the clouds are all drawn with the same rolling stroke.

Sargent asked to paint Virginie Gautreau, a Louisiana-born Paris socialite famous for her looks, and hoped the picture would make his name. It did, the wrong way: at the 1884 Salon the pose and the pallor caused a scandal, made worse by a jewelled strap that he had painted slipping off her shoulder.

He repainted the strap, moved to London, and kept the canvas for more than thirty years before selling it to the Met, telling the director it was perhaps the best thing he had done.

A woman rests one hand on a window and the other on a silver pitcher, and that is the whole event. What Vermeer is really painting is daylight: how it comes through the glass, turns the linen cap blue, and lands on the wall.

It was the first Vermeer to enter an American collection, given to the Met in 1889.

One of six panels of the seasons that Bruegel painted for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jongelinck; five survive. This is late summer. Some people are cutting wheat, others are eating and sleeping under a pear tree, and the land runs downhill all the way to the sea.

It is often called the first modern landscape, because the religious pretext is gone and the people are simply working.

One of the first pure landscapes in Spanish painting. El Greco lived in Toledo for half his life and here rearranges it to suit himself, moving the cathedral beside the Alcázar and setting the whole city under a sky that looks about to break.

Two dozen dancers and their mothers wait while the ballet master Jules Perrot conducts an examination. The rehearsal room is in the old Paris Opéra, which had burned down the year before, so Degas built the scene from memory and drawings.

Look at the edges: a dancer scratching her back, a watering can, a small dog.

title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
about:
The first print in the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, designed when Hokusai was about seventy. Three boats row into the wave; Fuji sits small and still in the hollow beneath it.

The blue is Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment then newly imported into Japan, and part of why the series sold so well.

Rembrandt at fifty-four, a few years after his bankruptcy, looking at himself without flattery: the heavy brow, the soft cheeks, the thick paint in the face and almost none in the clothes. He painted himself some forty times, and this is among the plainest.

Three models in Seurat’s studio, with A Sunday on La Grande Jatte leaning against the wall behind them. It was his answer to critics who said that painting in dots could never handle the nude.

At the Barnes it hangs in the Main Room directly above Cézanne’s Card Players, one of the great stacked pairs anywhere.

The largest of Cézanne’s five Card Players, and the most crowded. The models were farmhands from his family’s estate outside Aix. Nobody is winning or losing; the game is just a reason for five people to sit still while he works out how they fit together.

Joseph Roulin sorted mail at the railway station in Arles and became the closest friend Van Gogh had there. He painted Roulin six times, and here sets the blue uniform and the forked beard against a wallpaper of flowers.

Students leaving the Paris music conservatory stop on the pavement to talk. It is a large, early Renoir from the years of the first Impressionist exhibitions, when he was painting modern Parisians at life size.

Barnes went on to buy 181 Renoirs, more than anyone else has ever owned.

A bather is surprised by a bear; a hunter fires from the rocks. Rousseau was a retired Paris toll collector who taught himself to paint, and every leaf here gets the same patient attention as the drama in the middle.
Painted two years before Modigliani died at thirty-five. The long neck, the tilted head and the almond eyes are all his signature. Barnes bought his work early, when few American collectors would.

The mountain east of Aix-en-Provence that Cézanne painted dozens of times over twenty years. Here it is seen across the valley, put together from small patches of blue, green and ochre that read as distance without any drawn outline.

In August 1888 Van Gogh painted sunflowers to decorate the room where Gauguin would stay in Arles. That winter he made repetitions of the best ones, and this is one of them, painted in January 1889: twelve flowers at every stage from bud to seed head, on a turquoise ground.

Monet dug the pond at Giverny, planted it, built the arched bridge, and then in the summer of 1899 sat down and painted the same view of it again and again. The water garden would be his subject for the rest of his life.

On the night of October 16, 1834, the Houses of Parliament burned down, and Turner was in the crowd on the south bank of the Thames, sketching. He exhibited this a few months later. The fire fills half the canvas and its reflection most of the rest.

Tanner painted this after travelling in Egypt and Palestine. Mary is a girl in a plain room with rumpled bedclothes, and Gabriel is a column of light.

The museum bought it in 1899, the first of Tanner’s works to enter an American museum.

Among the first pictures Rousseau ever exhibited, at the Salon des Indépendants in 1886. Two figures in carnival costume stand at the edge of a bare winter wood under a full moon, lit from nowhere in particular.

Prometheus, punished for giving fire to people, is chained to a rock while an eagle tears at his liver. Rubens painted the figure and his friend Frans Snyders, the animal specialist, painted the eagle. Rubens kept it in his own house for years and counted it among his best.
About five inches by six, and painted on parchment. Inside that are two friars, a rocky wilderness, a walled city and a river with boats on it, all sharp enough to read under a magnifying glass.

Painted in the garden of the asylum at Saint-Rémy in May 1889, in Van Gogh’s first weeks there. Every flower is drawn individually, and one of them is white. His brother Theo sent it to the Salon des Indépendants that September.

The frame is the one it hangs in at the Getty.

One of some twenty-five canvases Monet made of the grain stacks in the field beside his house through the autumn and winter of 1890–91, changing canvases as the light changed. Fifteen were shown together in May 1891 and sold within days.
title: Wheatstacks, Snow Effect, Morning

about: Turner’s last painting of Rome, made ten years after his final visit: the Forum dissolving into evening light as the moon comes up. It has changed hands only a few times and is unusually well preserved.
title: Modern Rome – Campo Vaccino

about: A small self-portrait on copper, painted when Rembrandt was about twenty-two, dressed as a soldier and laughing. It was catalogued as the work of a follower until it surfaced at a country auction in England in 2007.

A young man in a red cap stands guard before a bastion, probably during the siege of Florence in 1529–30. Who he is has been argued over for a century. When the Getty bought it in 1989 it was the most expensive Old Master painting ever sold.
The actress Jeanne Demarsy as Spring, shown at the Salon of 1882 beside A Bar at the Folies-Bergère. Manet planned four seasons played by fashionable Parisian women and lived to finish two.

A young man leads a woman in white up a wooded path. Renoir was twenty-nine and working alongside Monet, and you can watch the brushwork start to come apart, four years before the first Impressionist exhibition.
The Sacramento Valley after rain: cattle, oaks, and a storm moving off. Bierstadt painted it in his New York studio from sketches made in California a few years earlier.

about: A double rainbow over an Andean gorge, assembled from Church’s travels in Ecuador and Jamaica. He painted it the year after the Civil War ended and after losing two children to diphtheria, and it is usually read as a picture of hope after a disaster.

about: Monet went to Venice once, in the autumn of 1908, and said it was too beautiful to be painted. Then he painted thirty-seven canvases. This one looks across the Grand Canal to Santa Maria della Salute.
